notes: Ruling slot 2 holds Baunsgaard's Danish Social Liberal Party with its MD sprite (MD had it in 16); Venstre therefore moves to slot 16 (starting popularity, economic liberalism) with its MD sprite. Coalition slot 1 is the Conservatives (real VKR partner). Slot 14: Inner Mission, then Christian People's Party from 1970.4.29 (KD sprite). Slot 20: Independent Party, then Glistrup's Progress Party from 1972.8.22 (MD FrP sprite). Slot 6 Tidehverv, 7 the Denmark-Soviet friendship association, 21 the DNSAP remnant under Salicath. Retsforbundet, Liberal Centre and the Schleswig Party are not placed.

0.name: Politiets Efterretningstjeneste
0.text:
Politiets Efterretningstjeneste is the security branch of the Danish police, built up after the liberation to guard against espionage and communist subversion in a country that joined NATO in 1949. It keeps files on members of the Communist Party, the Socialist People's Party, the Left Socialists and the new Maoist and student groups, and it closely watches Soviet and East German diplomats.

The service works hand in hand with military intelligence, the CIA and other allied services, and enjoys quiet cooperation from Social Democratic and trade-union officials who share its anti-communism. Its leverage lies in its registers, its surveillance powers and its access to ministers. In a grave crisis its officers would be the natural organisers of an emergency regime firmly anchored in the Atlantic alliance.

1.name: Det Konservative Folkeparti
1.text:
The Conservative People's Party, founded in 1916, won 20.4 percent and 37 seats in the January 1968 election, its best result in decades, and became the largest partner in the coalition of Venstre, the Conservatives and the Radicals headed by Hilmar Baunsgaard. Its leading figures in government are Finance Minister Poul Møller and Defence Minister Erik Ninn-Hansen.

The Conservatives stand for private enterprise, a sound economy, lower personal taxes, law and order and a strong national defence within NATO. They are the most determined advocates of Danish membership of the European Economic Community. Their base is the urban middle class, business and the professions of Copenhagen and its suburbs, and their leverage lies in holding the key economic ministries of the government.

2.name: Det Radikale Venstre
2.text:
The Danish Social Liberal Party, founded in 1905 by radicals who broke away from Venstre, leads the government through Hilmar Baunsgaard, Prime Minister since February 1968 of a coalition with Venstre and the Conservatives. The party doubled its vote to 15 percent and 27 seats in 1968, profiting from discontent with the Social Democrats.

The Radicals are social liberals with a long tradition of anti-militarism, internationalism and cultural freedom, and the coalition has made Denmark the first country to abolish censorship of pictorial pornography. They champion Nordic cooperation through the planned Nordek union, a cautious approach to the European Economic Community and modest defence budgets. Their base is teachers, smallholders and the educated middle class, and their leverage lies in the premiership itself.

3.name: Socialdemokratiet
3.text:
The Social Democrats, Denmark's largest party since 1924, governed for most of the post-war era and built the Danish welfare state. Jens Otto Krag, chairman since 1962 and Prime Minister from 1962 to 1968, now leads the opposition after the party fell to 34.2 percent in the 1968 election, losing votes both to the bourgeois parties and to the socialists on its left.

The party stands for full employment, universal welfare, economic management in partnership with the trade unions, and support for NATO and Danish entry into the European Economic Community. Its base is industrial workers, public employees and the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions under Thomas Nielsen. Its leverage lies in its size, its control of the labour movement and its long experience of government.

4.name: Danmarks Kommunistiske Parti
4.text:
Founded in 1919, the Communist Party of Denmark emerged from the occupation with great prestige and 18 seats in 1945, but the Cold War and the defection of its leader Aksel Larsen in 1958 shattered it. Chaired since 1958 by Knud Jespersen, it has had no seat in the Folketing since 1960 and won one percent in 1968. It publishes the daily Land og Folk.

The party demands Danish withdrawal from NATO, rejection of the European Economic Community, recognition of East Germany and North Vietnam, and nationalisation of the banks and monopolies. It remains loyal to the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact. Its base is older workers in Copenhagen's shipyards and docks, and its leverage lies in disciplined cells in several trade unions and in Soviet support.

5.name: Venstresocialisterne
5.text:
The Left Socialists were founded in December 1967 by members of the Socialist People's Party who refused to back the incomes policy of Jens Otto Krag's Social Democratic government, supported by their party in the so-called Red Cabinet. In the January 1968 election they won 2 percent and four seats, giving the New Left, the student revolt and the Vietnam movement a voice in the Folketing.

The party rejects both social democratic reformism and Soviet-style communism and calls for workers' councils, socialisation of the economy, withdrawal from NATO and a struggle against the European Economic Community. Its members range from libertarian socialists to Trotskyists and admirers of Third World revolutions, and its internal debates are fierce. Its leverage lies in the universities, the youth houses and radical shop stewards.

6.name: Tidehverv
6.text:
Tidehverv is a Lutheran theological movement founded in 1926 around the journal of the same name, which rejected pietism and liberal theology in favour of a stark reading of Luther and Kierkegaard. In the late 1960s a younger circle of theologians around Søren Krarup has turned it into the sharpest voice of national-conservative revolt against the spirit of 1968.

The movement denounces humanitarianism, the youth revolt, the welfare state's claim to redeem mankind and the cosmopolitan dream of European integration as idolatry. It defends the Danish people, the Danish language and the national church against Brussels, the ideology of the United Nations and Western progressive culture alike. Its leverage lies in its pulpits, its polemical journal and its influence on a generation of rural priests and teachers.

7.name: Landsforeningen Danmark-Sovjetunionen
7.text:
The Denmark–Soviet Union Association is the main friendship society for the Soviet Union in Denmark, closely tied to the Communist Party and to the Soviet embassy in Copenhagen. It organises delegations to Moscow and Leningrad, Soviet film weeks, language courses and exhibitions, and it draws in trade unionists, cultural figures and fellow travellers who admire the Soviet planned economy.

The association presents the Soviet Union as the guardian of peace and the Warsaw Pact's intervention in Czechoslovakia as a defence of socialism. It campaigns for Danish neutrality, the closure of the American bases in Greenland after the crash of a nuclear-armed bomber near Thule in 1968, and closer trade with the socialist countries. Its leverage lies in Soviet patronage and in a hard core ready to welcome a Moscow-aligned order.

8.name: Cem-kredsen
8.text:
The Cem Circle is a small group of Alevi workers from central Anatolia, among the Turkish labour migrants who have come to Copenhagen and its industrial suburbs since 1967. Far from home and from their dedes, the hereditary holy men of their faith, they gather in private flats for the cem ceremony of prayer, music and remembrance of Ali and the Twelve Imams.

The circle embodies a tolerant, heterodox Shia faith hostile to Sunni orthodoxy and to the religious nationalism of the Turkish right, and many members sympathise with Turkey's secular left and the Unity Party founded by Alevis in 1966. It values education, equality of men and women and good relations with Danes. Its leverage is minimal, resting on solidarity and links to Alevi villages at home.

9.name: Karbala-kredsen
9.text:
The Karbala Circle is a handful of Iraqi Shia students at the Technical University of Denmark and the University of Copenhagen, sons of merchant and clerical families from Karbala, Najaf and Baghdad who fear the growing repression of the Ba'athist regime. They study the writings of Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr and keep in touch with the underground Islamic Dawa Party.

The circle believes that the scholars of Islam must guide society and that only an Islamic state can save Muslims from Western capitalism, atheist communism and Ba'athist dictatorship alike. It reveres Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, as a model of clerical courage against tyranny. It has no legal existence or resources; its leverage lies only in the zeal of its members and their links to the seminaries of Iraq.

10.name: Ahmadiyya Muslim Jamaat
10.text:
The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community opened the Nusrat Djahan Mosque in the Copenhagen suburb of Hvidovre in 1967, the first purpose-built mosque in Scandinavia, paid for by donations from Ahmadi women around the world. Its missionary work in Scandinavia began in the 1950s, and the movement is led worldwide by its third Caliph, Mirza Nasir Ahmad, from Rabwah in Pakistan.

The community preaches a peaceful, missionary Islam, rejects armed jihad and demands loyalty to the laws of the host country. It wins a trickle of Danish converts and serves as the public face of Islam in Denmark, although orthodox Sunni scholars regard its claims about its founder as heresy. Its leverage lies in discipline, international organisation and the only purpose-built mosque in the country.

11.name: Tahrir-studenterne
11.text:
The Tahrir Students are a few Palestinian and Jordanian students at Danish universities who carry the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and banned across the Arab world. Since the Six-Day War they argue that the defeat of the Arab regimes proves the bankruptcy of nationalism and socialism alike.

The group demands the restoration of a single caliphate that would unite all Muslims, apply the sharia in full and confront both Western and Soviet power, and it rejects participation in any secular political system. It relies on study circles, leaflets and persuasion rather than violence. In Denmark its leverage is negligible; its significance lies in the dedicated cadres it trains for the Arab world.

12.name: Qutb-kredsen
12.text:
The Qutb Circle is a small group of Egyptian, Syrian and Pakistani students and workers in Copenhagen who read Sayyid Qutb, the Muslim Brotherhood thinker hanged by Nasser in 1966, together with Hasan al-Banna and Abul A'la Maududi. They meet for Friday prayers in rented rooms and correspond with Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva, the Brotherhood's main outpost in Europe.

The circle calls for an Islamic renewal that rejects both capitalism and communism, for solidarity with Palestine after the defeat of 1967 and for Muslim migrants to preserve their faith in a permissive society. It works through education, mutual aid and preaching rather than confrontation, and keeps a careful distance from the Ahmadiyya mission. Its leverage lies in organisation and in the growing number of Muslim guest workers.

13.name: Slotsholmens mandariner
13.text:
Slotsholmens mandariner are the senior civil servants and economists of the ministries on Slotsholmen, the island in central Copenhagen that houses the government, together with the experts of the Economic Council, whose independent 'wise men' have advised governments since 1962, and the National Bank under Erik Hoffmeyer. They draft budgets, incomes policies and long-term plans for whichever coalition holds office.

The mandarins believe that economic management is too important to be left to party bargaining and that wage restraint, balance-of-payments discipline and rational planning must be imposed from above. Their horizon is the national economy, not the bloc confrontation. Their leverage lies in expertise, continuity and the dependence of every short-lived minister on their files and forecasts.

14.name: Kirkelig Forening for den Indre Mission i Danmark
14.native_full: Kirkelig Forening for den Indre Mission i Danmark
14.text:
The Inner Mission, founded in 1861, is the largest revival movement within the Danish national church, with its mission houses, youth societies and schools concentrated in western and northern Jutland and on Bornholm. It shapes daily life in hundreds of parishes through Bible study, temperance and strict Sunday observance, and it has always worked inside the church and through the existing parties.

The movement is outraged by the liberalisation of abortion, the legalisation of pornography, the decline of Christian education and what it sees as the moral bankruptcy of the welfare state. Many of its members now discuss founding a Christian party of their own. Its leverage lies in a dense network of devout communities, a loyal press and the votes it can move between parties.

14.name: Kristeligt Folkeparti
14.text:
The Christian People's Party is founded in April 1970 by laymen from the Inner Mission and other revival circles in protest against the legalisation of pornography, the liberalisation of abortion and the decline of Christian values in schools. It is the first explicitly Christian party in Danish national politics and sets out to enter the Folketing at the next election.

The party demands a ban on pornography, restrictions on abortion, Christian education, support for the family and strict alcohol policies, combined with a moderate, welfare-minded economic programme. It is wary of European integration as a vehicle of materialism. Its base is the devout communities of western Jutland and the revival movements, and its leverage lies in a disciplined electorate that can tip the balance between the blocs.

15.name: A.P. Møller-gruppen
15.text:
The A.P. Møller Group is Denmark's largest business empire, built around the Maersk Line shipping company, the Odense Steel Shipyard at Lindø and a web of industrial holdings. Since the death of its founder Arnold Peter Møller in 1965 it has been run by his son Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller, a reserved and immensely influential figure in Danish public life.

In 1962 the group won the sole concession to explore the Danish subsoil for oil and gas, and it now leads the Danish Underground Consortium with international oil companies in the North Sea. It stands for free trade, low taxes, Danish entry into the European Economic Community and a firmly Western orientation. Its leverage lies in shipping, oil and capital that no Danish government can ignore.

16.name: Venstre, Danmarks Liberale Parti
16.text:
Venstre, Denmark's Liberal Party, was founded in 1870 as the party of the farmers against the landowners and the Crown and won parliamentary government in 1901. Led since 1965 by Poul Hartling, now Foreign Minister, it won 18.6 percent and 34 seats in 1968 and sits in Hilmar Baunsgaard's coalition with the Conservatives and the Radicals.

Venstre is the party of economic liberalism: free trade, low taxes, private property, limited government and resistance to socialist planning and high public spending. It firmly supports NATO and has long pushed for Danish membership of the European Economic Community to secure markets for Danish farm exports. Its base is independent farmers, rural towns and small businesses, and its leverage lies in its rural organisation and its place in government.

17.name: Danmarks Naturfredningsforening
17.text:
Founded in 1911, the Danish Society for Nature Conservation is Denmark's largest green organisation, with the legal right to propose protection orders for landscapes, coasts and monuments. As the European Conservation Year opens, it is turning its attention from scenic preservation to the pollution of the Øresund, the fjords and the air of the industrial towns.

The society demands strict controls on industrial waste and agricultural chemicals, protection of the dunes, heaths and beaches from summer-house sprawl and motorways, and public access to nature. A new generation of student activists is pressing it towards a radical critique of growth and consumption. Its leverage lies in its broad membership, its legal standing in conservation cases and the Danish attachment to the countryside.

18.name: Socialistisk Folkeparti
18.text:
The Socialist People's Party was founded in 1959 by Aksel Larsen, the former Communist leader expelled for his independent line after the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising. It won 11 seats in 1968 after losing its left wing to the Left Socialists; Sigurd Ømann now chairs the party, while Larsen remains its elder statesman.

The party seeks a democratic socialism independent of Moscow: public control of banks and big business, workers' influence in industry, an expanded welfare state and Danish withdrawal from NATO in favour of Nordic neutrality. It opposes membership of the European Economic Community. Its base is skilled workers, teachers and students, and its leverage lies in its role as the necessary partner of any Social Democratic majority.

19.name: Kommunistisk Forbund Marxister-Leninister
19.text:
The Communist League of Marxist-Leninists was formed in 1968 by young Maoists from the student and Vietnam movements who reject the Communist Party of Denmark as revisionist. The historian Benito Scocozza is among its leading figures, and it competes fiercely with Gotfred Appel's older Communist Working Circle for recognition from Peking.

The league upholds Mao Zedong Thought and the Cultural Revolution, denounces Soviet social-imperialism and American imperialism alike and calls for a revolutionary workers' party to overthrow Danish capitalism. It opposes NATO and Danish entry into the European Economic Community. Its leverage lies in the dedication of its young cadres, its influence in the Vietnam committees and the universities, and its efforts to build cells in the factories.

20.name: De Uafhængige
20.text:
The Independent Party was founded in the early 1950s by dissident Conservatives who believed their old party had made its peace with the Social Democratic welfare state. It once held a few seats in the Folketing but is now out of parliament and won only half a percent in the 1968 election.

The party campaigns against high taxes, bureaucracy, public spending and the power of the trade unions, and it defends property owners, small businessmen and independent farmers against the expanding state. It is fiercely anti-communist and suspicious of the bourgeois coalition, which it accuses of continuing Social Democratic policies. Its leverage lies in a reservoir of tax resentment that the established parties have failed to address.

20.name: Fremskridtspartiet
20.text:
The Progress Party is founded in August 1972 by Mogens Glistrup, a Copenhagen tax lawyer who became a national celebrity by declaring on television that he paid no income tax and comparing tax evaders to the saboteurs of the wartime resistance. Its rallies draw crowds of angry taxpayers from every class and region.

The party demands the abolition of income tax, drastic cuts in bureaucracy and public spending, an end to foreign aid and the replacement of the armed forces by an answering machine saying 'we surrender' in Russian. Its style is provocative and anti-establishment. Its leverage lies in a massive protest vote against high taxes and against all the old parties.

21.name: Danmarks Nationalsocialistiske Arbejderparti
21.english: National Socialist Workers' Party of Denmark
21.text:
The National Socialist Workers' Party of Denmark was the Nazi party of Frits Clausen, which collaborated with the German occupiers and collapsed in disgrace in 1945. A tiny band of veterans has kept the name alive under Svend Salicath, publishing the paper Fædrelandet since 1952, with a few dozen members and almost no public presence.

The party venerates Hitler's National Socialism, denies the crimes of the occupation regime and preaches racial nationalism, anti-Semitism and hatred of communism and liberal democracy. It rejects both American and Soviet power in the name of a Nordic racial community. Its leverage is close to nil, though it attracts a handful of young admirers and keeps up contacts with neo-Nazi networks abroad.
21.wiki: National Socialist Workers' Party of Denmark

22.name: Forsvaret
22.text:
The Danish Defence comprises the army, navy and air force, built on conscription and integrated into NATO's command for the Baltic Approaches, which guards the straits between the Baltic and the North Sea against the Warsaw Pact fleets. The officer corps serves under the Chief of Defence and Defence Minister Erik Ninn-Hansen of the Conservative People's Party.

The officers are loyal to the King and the constitution and have no tradition of political intervention, but they resent the Radicals' anti-militarism and the pressure for defence cuts, and they distrust the pacifist left. Should Denmark face invasion or internal breakdown, the armed forces would become the guarantors of an emergency order. Their leverage lies in conscription, the Home Guard and their close ties to NATO allies.

23.name: Huset Glücksborg
23.text:
The House of Glücksburg has reigned in Denmark since 1863, when Christian IX succeeded the last king of the Oldenburg line. King Frederik IX, on the throne since 1947, is a popular, informal monarch and a keen amateur conductor; since the Act of Succession of 1953 his eldest daughter Princess Margrethe, married in 1967 to the French diplomat Henri de Laborde de Monpezat, is heir to the throne.

The Crown stands above parties and exercises no political power under the 1953 constitution, but it embodies national continuity and the memory of Christian X's quiet defiance during the occupation. Monarchist sentiment is nearly universal. In a crisis the King's moral authority and the loyalty of the armed forces to the Crown would carry great weight.
